title: Quote Revision Vault
user: A solo service provider who needs to revise a quote without losing what was previously offered or accidentally billing against the wrong version.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Invoice Ninja user explicitly asks for a revision on every save after overwriting something by mistake, with rollback depth.
A freelancer says the only desired functions were simple quoting, invoicing, and recurring invoices—evidence that a small, focused workflow is preferable to a suite.

recurrence: Two independent freelancer/invoicing contexts; accidental changes are high-severity because the sent price and scope become difficult to prove.
current_workaround: Duplicate a PDF, rename files with v2/v3, or trust a suite's generic audit log and manually compare PDFs.
incumbents_and_gap: Invoice Ninja, QuickBooks, and Xero create quotes but make a compact before/after scope-and-price comparison and customer-facing version receipt secondary or absent.
smallest_useful_product: Offline-first quote editor that stores immutable revisions, renders a line-item diff, and exports one PDF plus a customer-acknowledgement link. Non-goals: payments, bookkeeping, e-signature legality, or a CRM.
success_measure: In a 30-day pilot, 70% of users who revise a quote send the generated diff, and at least one avoids a scope/price clarification email.
monetization: one-time — quote history is durable local business data and should keep working without a recurring bill.
constraints: Keep quote/customer data local by default; link tokens must be revocable and expiry-controlled; do not represent acknowledgement as a legally binding signature.
why_distinct: The primary artifact is an intelligible revision trail, not a full invoicing product.

title: Quote Approval Receipt
user: A small agency or contractor who needs a defensible record of which client contact approved a quote when approval happens outside a client portal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A self-hosted Invoice Ninja user asks to record who approved a quote or paid an invoice because staff currently appear as approvers when they only mark status.
A freelancer asks how to handle a client who does not give approval but later changes expectations, exposing the cost of missing approval evidence.

recurrence: Two independent contractor workflows; this becomes severe when a disputed scope, purchase approval, or payment is attributed to the wrong person.
current_workaround: Save scattered email screenshots, forward a WhatsApp message to oneself, or have staff manually mark a quote approved.
incumbents_and_gap: PandaDoc, DocuSign, and CRM suites are heavier than the need; Invoice Ninja's status can record the operator rather than the actual approver.
smallest_useful_product: A tiny share-link page that displays an immutable quote snapshot, asks approver name/title and a clear approve/request-changes choice, then issues a timestamped PDF receipt. Non-goals: legally regulated e-signatures, payment collection, or proposal authoring.
success_measure: At least 80% of pilot approvals include a named external approver, with fewer than 5% requiring manual follow-up to identify the decision maker.
monetization: freemium — a low-volume free tier supports solo contractors; branded domains and retention are paid needs.
constraints: Make consent language configurable; protect share links from indexing; retain minimal PII and offer export/deletion; do not claim signature-law compliance.
why_distinct: It captures approval provenance from an existing quote rather than replacing proposal, signing, or CRM software.

title: Deposit Deadline Bridge
user: An event, catering, or project business that quotes a deposit and final balance and needs those independently negotiated dates to survive conversion to an invoice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A catering/event business reports that quote-to-invoice conversion loses custom deposit and final-payment deadlines and reverts to generic NET terms.
A freelancer asks specifically about planning payment milestones, demonstrating the separate scheduling problem beyond issuing one invoice.

recurrence: Two independent service-business contexts; missed deposits can make committed work or event purchasing cash-negative.
current_workaround: Put due dates in free-text quote notes, maintain a spreadsheet reminder list, or manually create separate invoices after acceptance.
incumbents_and_gap: Invoice Ninja, Xero, and QuickBooks support invoices and payment terms, but conversion commonly collapses a bespoke deposit/final schedule into one general term.
smallest_useful_product: A local quote attachment that defines deposit/final milestones, emits calendar files and reminder emails, and exports two clear payment instructions for any accounting system. Non-goals: card processing, debt collection, and general project management.
success_measure: During a 60-day pilot, 90% of accepted quotes with deposits have both deadlines recorded and no deadline is retyped after invoice creation.
monetization: one-time — this is a narrow, durable cash-flow utility that can operate with the user's own email/calendar.
constraints: Never send payment reminders without user confirmation; store dates/time zones precisely; locale-specific invoice and late-fee rules must remain user-configured.
why_distinct: It preserves a two-stage cash commitment across tools instead of becoming another invoice generator.

title: Client Catalogue Request
user: A tiny B2B seller that already maintains a product list and needs approved clients to request a quote or reorder without a full ecommerce store.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A self-hosted user asks for client-portal product selection that can request quotes or create/pay invoices, including visible-price and POA items.
An import/export reseller describes manual orders, payments, stock handling, in-stock versus preorder items, and asks for barcode/product support.

recurrence: Two separate small-selling contexts; manual reorders and quote requests consume time but a full storefront is disproportionate.
current_workaround: Accept email/WhatsApp orders, send a PDF catalogue, then re-key product lines into an invoice or ERP.
incumbents_and_gap: Shopify and WooCommerce are storefronts; Odoo/ERP systems are broad. Neither is optimized for a deliberately small, approved-client request list with POA and stock caveats.
smallest_useful_product: A shareable, passwordless client catalogue imported from CSV with request-for-quote basket, POA items, stock note, and CSV/PDF handoff to the seller. Non-goals: checkout, public marketplace SEO, fulfillment, or inventory accounting.
success_measure: A pilot seller receives 50% of repeat requests as structured baskets and reduces re-keyed line items by at least 75% in one month.
monetization: subscription — hosted client links, delivery, and access control have ongoing operating cost.
constraints: Avoid exposing stock counts or customer pricing by default; protect client links; make tax/pricing labels configurable; no payment-card handling in v1.
why_distinct: It is a request layer between a PDF catalogue and a commerce stack, not a Shopify clone.

title: MTD Evidence Pack
user: A UK sole trader using local bookkeeping who needs a quarter-by-quarter evidence pack and a clear readiness checklist before handing data to compatible filing software or an accountant.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A long-time self-hosted Invoice Ninja user says MTD requirements are forcing a move to Xero/QuickBooks despite already having customers, invoices, and expenses.
A UK sole-trader bookkeeping project is explicitly built around MTD ITSA changes and a first quarterly deadline; a commenter objects to being forced through third parties.

recurrence: Two current UK sources directly cite MTD-driven displacement; compliance deadlines make the pain acute and time-bound.
current_workaround: Move all books to a subscription suite, build a spreadsheet, or repeatedly chase an accountant for what needs to be handed over.
incumbents_and_gap: Xero, QuickBooks, FreeAgent, and MTD bridges submit or manage books; they do not offer a simple local, tool-neutral pre-flight and accountant-ready evidence pack.
smallest_useful_product: Local PWA that imports categorized CSV transactions, checks completeness against a user-maintained period checklist, and exports a read-only ZIP/CSV/PDF handoff. Non-goals: HMRC API submission, tax calculation advice, bank aggregation, or legal certification.
success_measure: Ten pilot sole traders produce an accountant-acceptable quarterly handoff in under 30 minutes with no repeated request for a missing source document.
monetization: one-time — compliance preparation should not require a new recurring platform and can remain entirely local.
constraints: Clearly state it is not tax advice or filing software; version jurisdiction-specific checklists; encrypt local exports; avoid storing HMRC credentials.
why_distinct: It reduces lock-in at the evidence-preparation boundary rather than competing to be a regulated accounting or filing suite.

title: Unbilled Work Sweep
user: A freelancer or tiny agency that records tasks or time in more than one tool and needs a weekly, local view of completed work that has not yet reached an invoice.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Invoice Ninja user asks for a dashboard total of non-invoiced tasks, showing that unbilled work is not visible enough in the main workflow.
A bookkeeping/invoicing worker asks for fast, keyboard-first internal tools and commenters emphasize repetitive workflow efficiency and lower error rates.

recurrence: Two 2025–26 business-software requests; unbilled completed work directly delays cash collection and is easy to miss in task-heavy weeks.
current_workaround: Open task, time, and invoice screens side-by-side, run ad-hoc reports, or maintain a manual 'invoice next' tag.
incumbents_and_gap: Harvest, Toggl, Kimai, and Invoice Ninja track time or invoices, but cross-tool 'what needs human billing attention now?' is not their compact default view.
smallest_useful_product: Local CSV importer for task/time/invoice exports that matches client/project names, lists unmatched completed work, and produces an invoice-draft checklist. Non-goals: time tracking, invoicing, payroll, or live account integrations in v1.
success_measure: Pilot users identify at least 95% of their completed-but-unbilled value in a weekly sweep and reduce average billing lag by seven days.
monetization: one-time — local import and reconciliation has episodic value without requiring a hosted account.
constraints: All imports stay on-device; matching suggestions must be reviewable; do not infer taxable income or alter source records.
why_distinct: It is an attention queue built from existing exports, not another time tracker or invoicing platform.

title: Barcode Intake Card
user: A micro-seller or workshop receiving miscellaneous stock who needs to turn a barcode scan into a reviewable item card without sending supplier or inventory data to a third party.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An InvenTree user says an unknown DigiKey barcode only produces 'no match' and requests a scan flow that pre-fills or merges a new part; the API workaround feels hacky.
A developer describes small businesses and ecommerce sellers needing bulk barcode labels but rejecting costly enterprise subscriptions and CSV uploads to free generators.

recurrence: Two 2025–26 inventory sources; unknown-item intake is recurring, while data disclosure and enterprise label pricing are explicit friction.
current_workaround: Type details manually, use a generic barcode lookup, upload a CSV to a label site, or write one-off API scripts.
incumbents_and_gap: InvenTree and Odoo manage inventory; BarTender prints labels. The missing lightweight piece is scan-to-review intake that creates a portable item card before adopting an ERP.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA scanner with manual/CSV lookup, photo and supplier fields, duplicate-candidate review, and printable one-up label/card export. Non-goals: warehouse management, automatic web scraping, purchase orders, or a universal product database.
success_measure: A pilot can record 30 miscellaneous items in under an hour with at least 90% having a searchable barcode and location note.
monetization: one-time — camera scanning and local label generation have no necessary hosted-service cost.
constraints: Offline camera permissions only; preserve user photos locally; barcode lookups must be opt-in and disclose third-party requests; use properly licensed barcode libraries.
why_distinct: It solves the uncertain first intake step before a business needs a stock system, rather than cloning an ERP or label suite.

title: Stock Return Trail
user: A field-service team or tiny maker with a main store and temporary personal/job locations who needs to return unused stock to the exact origin without reconstructing its history.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An InvenTree user explains that returning unused work-trip materials requires manually finding each item's previous location and asks for prefilled 'transfer back.'
A physical-product seller asks for tools to manage inventory across warehouses and forecasting, illustrating the operational cost of stock dispersed between locations.

recurrence: A current feature request documents the exact manual workaround; separate inventory-operations discussion confirms multi-location stock is a persistent small-business problem.
current_workaround: Search old movement records or inventory screens item-by-item, then manually transfer each unused item back.
incumbents_and_gap: InvenTree, Sortly, and Odoo track stock, but return-to-origin is often a generic transfer rather than a fast job-closeout workflow with provenance prefilled.
smallest_useful_product: Offline mobile PWA with scan-out to a job/location, a job-closeout screen that proposes each item's origin, partial-use counts, and a CSV movement log. Non-goals: procurement, demand planning, multi-user ERP synchronization, or accounting valuation.
success_measure: In pilots, 80% of returns are recorded at closeout and the median time to reconcile a field kit falls below ten minutes.
monetization: one-time — a site-kit utility has local data and predictable, small-team usage.
constraints: Explain that movement logs are not audit-grade inventory valuation; provide export/backup; conflict handling is required before adding shared-device sync.
why_distinct: It is a return-provenance workflow for temporary stock, not a general inventory system.

title: Paid Before Ship Gate
user: A tiny seller that quotes or takes orders on flexible terms but needs a visible, intentional rule for which orders must be paid before they are packed or dispatched.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An InvenTree user asks for sale-order payment status, outstanding-payment totals, and an optional paid-before-shipping gate because current orders assume payment.
A business asks how to handle a client that never pays a monthly invoice on time; responses recommend prepayment and clear late-payment communication.

recurrence: A 2026 inventory request gives an exact ship-gate use case, while an independent client-payment discussion shows the cash-loss consequence of weak controls.
current_workaround: Use a spreadsheet column, remember customer exceptions, or stop shipments manually after an overdue invoice is noticed.
incumbents_and_gap: Shopify, QuickBooks, and ERPs manage payment/order states, but their workflows are often too broad for a simple, exception-aware packing decision fed by a CSV export.
smallest_useful_product: Local order-status board that imports orders and payment confirmations, flags 'hold until paid' rules by customer/order, logs an override reason, and exports a pack list. Non-goals: payment processing, credit scoring, debt collection, inventory reservation, or shipping labels.
success_measure: Across one month, no order marked hold is dispatched without either recorded payment or a named override, while pack-list preparation takes under five minutes per batch.
monetization: one-time — it is a local operational guardrail, not a transaction platform.
constraints: Payment imports are sensitive; support redacted CSV columns and device encryption; do not make creditworthiness claims or automatically contact customers.
why_distinct: It adds a lightweight decision checkpoint between payment evidence and packing, rather than recreating order management.

title: Bills Due Board
user: A solo operator who records bills in a personal/business finance tool but needs a clear due-date queue and an intentional 'paid' action when cash becomes available.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Firefly III user asks for incoming invoices listed by due date and manually marked paid; their workaround creates an 'invoices due' account and two transactions per invoice.
A small-business user reports accounting/payroll filing errors and asks for an alternative with reliable records and professional sharing, emphasizing the risk of opaque finance workflows.

recurrence: A current self-hosted finance request states the exact queue problem; independent small-business accounting pain reinforces the need for transparent, reviewable records.
current_workaround: Create artificial clearing accounts, maintain a spreadsheet, or scan calendar/email reminders while separately entering payment transactions.
incumbents_and_gap: Firefly III, QuickBooks, and Xero have finance data but do not all make a small manual-bill queue with simple payment confirmation a focused local-first artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Offline bills board with manual/CSV entry, due-date and cash-week views, attachment links, paid confirmation, and export back to CSV. Non-goals: bank syncing, accounting ledger posting, payment initiation, or tax advice.
success_measure: Pilot users enter 90% of payable bills into one queue and can identify every bill due in the next seven days in under one minute.
monetization: one-time — users who want this view often prefer not to hand financial data to another SaaS.
constraints: No bank credentials; encrypted local storage and export; clearly distinguish planned bills from cleared accounting transactions.
why_distinct: It is a payable-attention layer that complements a ledger instead of claiming to be accounting software.

title: Subscription Renewal Calendar
user: A small business that pays many SaaS and operating subscriptions and needs to see upcoming renewals, rising costs, and a human owner before the next charge.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Firefly III user reports that repeated weekly subscriptions in one month disappear from the expected-payment total and 'subscriptions to pay' widget.
A small-business subscription-tracker discussion asks about tracking AWS, OpenAI, email, and marketing-tool expenses, especially which costs are growing.

recurrence: Two 2025–26 finance-tool contexts; recurring charges are easy to overlook, and broken recurrence math makes a monthly total unsafe to trust.
current_workaround: Use a spreadsheet or personal subscription app, search bank transactions, or rely on calendar reminders with no amount/owner context.
incumbents_and_gap: Rocket Money, Ramp, Firefly III, and bank feeds track charges, but small teams need a local import-first renewal calendar with owner and cancel/keep decision—not expense-management infrastructure.
smallest_useful_product: Offline CSV-first renewal calendar that models weekly/monthly/annual schedules, displays every occurrence, assigns an owner and review date, and exports ICS reminders. Non-goals: bank connections, procurement approvals, card management, or AI categorization.
success_measure: In a 60-day pilot, users assign an owner to 80% of recurring spend and catch every renewal above a chosen threshold at least seven days early.
monetization: one-time — a local calendar and CSV import should be useful without a bank-data subscription.
constraints: Recurring-date calculations must cover multiple same-month occurrences and time zones; no financial credentials; provide encrypted export and deletion.
why_distinct: It turns recurring spend into a decision calendar, not a generic spend dashboard or an LLM receipt wrapper.

title: Client Exit Packet
user: A freelance developer or small agency completing a client engagement who needs to hand over assets, access instructions, known issues, and support boundaries in one acknowledged packet.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A subcontractor asks to distinguish the party billed from the end client across clients, projects, tasks, and invoices because the relationship otherwise ends up in free text or nowhere.
A freelancer asks how to hand off an iPhone app, source, Apple signing, and financial account responsibilities to a client who cannot compile or sign it themselves.

recurrence: A current subcontractor workflow and an independent app-handoff question identify the same gap: a transfer of files is not a transfer of operational understanding, client context, or responsibility.
current_workaround: Email a ZIP and a long checklist, hold an unrecorded call, share credentials insecurely, or leave support expectations undocumented.
incumbents_and_gap: Notion, Google Drive, 1Password, and project-management tools store parts of the handoff, but do not produce a scoped, client-acknowledged exit packet with explicit outstanding items and support boundary.
smallest_useful_product: Local encrypted packet builder with asset/access checklist, known-issues register, support end date, redacted credential references, and a read-only acknowledgement page/PDF. Non-goals: credential vaulting, source-code hosting, e-signature compliance, or ongoing support desk.
success_measure: At least 80% of pilot handoffs receive a client acknowledgement and generate no repeated 'where is/what does this do?' request during the first two weeks.
monetization: one-time — a reusable offboarding artifact fits project-based work and must remain accessible after a contractor leaves.
constraints: Never include plaintext secrets by default; encrypt local packets; make expiry/revocation clear; do not promise legal release or signature validity.
why_distinct: It packages a bounded operational transition and acknowledgement rather than trying to replace documents, passwords, or a client portal.
